claim: Transmembrane domains (TMDs) engage in protein-protein interactions that regulate many cellular processes.
source: Transmembrane domains (TMDs) engage in protein-protein interactions that regulate many cellular processes, but the rules governing the specificity of these interactions are poorly understood.
evidence: This is a general statement about TMDs supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The rules governing the specificity of TMD interactions are poorly understood.
source: Transmembrane domains (TMDs) engage in protein-protein interactions that regulate many cellular processes, but the rules governing the specificity of these interactions are poorly understood.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field and provides context for the study.

claim: 26-residue model transmembrane proteins consisting exclusively of leucine and isoleucine (LIL traptamers) specifically activate the erythropoietin receptor (EPOR) in mouse cells to confer growth factor independence.
source: To discover these principles, we analyzed 26-residue model transmembrane proteins consisting exclusively of leucine and isoleucine (called LIL traptamers) that specifically activate the erythropoietin receptor (EPOR) in mouse cells to confer growth factor independence.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The placement of a single side chain methyl group at specific positions in a traptamer determined whether it associated productively with the TMD of the human EPOR, the mouse EPOR, or both receptors.
source: We discovered that the placement of a single side chain methyl group at specific positions in a traptamer determined whether it associated productively with the TMD of the human EPOR, the mouse EPOR, or both receptors.
evidence: This is a key finding supported by mutational analysis data shown in Figure 2C and other experiments.

claim: Association of the traptamers with the EPOR induced EPOR oligomerization in an orientation that stimulated receptor activity.
source: Association of the traptamers with the EPOR induced EPOR oligomerization in an orientation that stimulated receptor activity.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 3D) and NMR data (Figure 4).

claim: A single methyl group can dictate the specificity of TMD interactions.
source: These results highlight the high intrinsic specificity of TMD interactions, demonstrate that a single methyl group can dictate specificity, and define the minimal chemical difference that can modulate the specificity of TMD interactions and the activity of transmembrane proteins.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the mutational analysis data showing that single leucine-isoleucine substitutions alter specificity.

claim: Integral membrane proteins constitute ~30% of the proteome of eukaryotic cells.
source: Integral membrane proteins constitute ~30% of the proteome of eukaryotic cells and serve many important biological functions (Lehnert et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lehnert et al., 2004.

claim: TMDs can align laterally in the membrane and oligomerize via hydrogen bonds, salt-bridges, or van der Waals packing interactions.
source: TMDs can align laterally in the membrane and oligomerize via hydrogen bonds, salt-bridges, or van der Waals packing interactions (Langosch and Arkin, 2009; Moore et al., 2008; Bugge et al., 2016; Choma et al., 2000; Zhou et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The E5 oncoprotein of bovine papillomavirus (BPV) is a homodimeric, single-pass 44-residue TM protein that binds specifically to the TMD of the platelet-derived growth factor β receptor (PDGFβR).
source: The functional relevance of a free-standing TMD is illustrated by the E5 oncoprotein of bovine papillomavirus (BPV), a homodimeric, single-pass 44-residue TM protein that binds specifically to the TMD of the platelet-derived growth factor β receptor (PDGFβR), resulting in sustained receptor activation and cell transformation (Lai et al., 1998; Petti et al., 1991; Schlegel et al., 1986; Goldstein et al., 1992; Petti and DiMaio, 1992; Talbert-Slagle and DiMaio, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work on the E5 oncoprotein.

claim: Traptamers are small (<50 residues), biologically active artificial TM proteins.
source: To study the interactions between TMDs, we developed a genetic system to isolate small (<50 residues), biologically active artificial TM proteins named traptamers (Freeman-Cook and DiMaio, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Freeman-Cook and DiMaio, 2005, which describes the development of traptamers.

claim: The EPOR is a single-pass TM protein that exists in a monomer-dimer equilibrium in unstimulated cells.
source: The EPOR is a single-pass TM protein that exists in a monomer-dimer equilibrium in unstimulated cells and is driven toward a productive dimeric form by EPO binding (Constantinescu et al., 2001; Ebie and Fleming, 2007; Kubatzky et al., 2001; Livnah et al., 1999; Moraga et al., 2015; Ruan et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work on EPOR structure and function.

claim: Ligand-induced dimerization of the EPOR in the proper orientation results in autophosphorylation of constitutively bound JAK2 kinases.
source: Ligand-induced dimerization of the EPOR in the proper orientation results in autophosphorylation of constitutively bound JAK2 kinases, phosphorylation of the intracellular domain of the EPOR, and initiation of intracellular signaling cascades (Seubert et al., 2003; Syed et al., 1998; Witthuhn et al., 1993; Remy et al., 1999; Watowich, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work on EPOR signaling.

claim: The mouse EPOR (mEPOR) but not the hEPOR is activated by gp55-P, a 55 kDa viral TM protein.
source: The mouse EPOR (mEPOR) but not the hEPOR is also activated by gp55-P, a 55 kDa viral TM protein with a large, glycosylated extracellular domain (Li et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Li et al., 1990.

claim: Point mutations in the TMDs of gp55-P and the mEPOR can prevent EPOR activation.
source: Point mutations in the TMDs of gp55-P and the mEPOR can prevent EPOR activation (Amanuma et al., 1989; Chung et al., 1989; Zon et al., 1992; Constantinescu et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: 26-residue traptamers consisting of only leucines and isoleucines (LIL traptamers) can specifically activate the PDGFβR and transform cells.
source: Remarkably, we discovered that 26-residue traptamers consisting of only leucines and isoleucines following an initiating methionine (LIL traptamers) can specifically activate the PDGFβR and transform cells (Heim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Heim et al., 2015.

claim: LIL traptamers define the minimal chemical complexity required to generate an active protein.
source: Because these proteins are comprised exclusively of two hydrophobic amino acids that differ chemically only by the placement of a single side chain methyl group and cannot undergo post-translational modification, these results defined the minimal chemical complexity required to generate an active protein.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the properties of LIL traptamers and their biological activity.

claim: The UDv6 library expresses LIL traptamers in which a methionine initiation codon is followed by 25 codons encoding equimolar leucine and isoleucine in a random order.
source: The UDv6 library expresses LIL traptamers in which a methionine initiation codon is followed by 25 codons encoding equimolar leucine and isoleucine in a random order (Heim et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the library used in the study, supported by a citation to Heim et al., 2015.

claim: Five LIL traptamers stimulated IL-3-independent growth of BaF3/hEPOR cells but not parental BaF3 cells.
source: Five LIL traptamers stimulated IL-3-independent growth of BaF3/hEPOR cells but not parental BaF3 cells (Figure 2A), demonstrating that the EPOR was required for the activity of these traptamers.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Traptamers LH1, LH2, LH3, and LH4 cooperated with the hEPOR but not with the mEPOR.
source: Although traptamers LH1, LH2, LH3, and LH4 cooperated with the hEPOR, they did not cooperate with the mEPOR, highlighting the high specificity of these traptamers.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: LH5 cooperated with both the mEPOR and the hEPOR.
source: In contrast, LH5 cooperated with both the mEPOR and the hEPOR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Neither LH1 nor LH5 induced IL-3 independence in cells expressing hEPOR/F8, a phosphorylation-defective mutant of the hEPOR.
source: Neither LH1 nor LH5 induced IL-3 independence in cells expressing hEPOR/F8, a phosphorylation-defective mutant of the hEPOR that does not support EPO-induced proliferation (Wu et al., 1997) (Figure 2B), suggesting that activation of the EPOR and its downstream signaling pathways were required for traptamer-induced cell proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and a citation to Wu et al., 1997.

claim: Neither LH1 nor LH5 induced IL-3 independence in cells expressing the PDGFβR or the SCFR.
source: To assess specificity, we also co-expressed LH1 and LH5 with the PDGFβR or the stem cell factor receptor (SCFR), two receptor tyrosine kinases unrelated to the EPOR. Neither traptamer induced IL-3 independence in cells expressing these receptors, even though these cells proliferated in response to their cognate ligands (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The LIL traptamers specifically activated the EPOR.
source: Thus, the LIL traptamers studied here specifically activated the EPOR.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the data showing that traptamers do not activate other receptors.

claim: The substitutions L9I and I10L in LH5 dramatically changed the specificity of LH5.
source: Most interestingly, the substitutions L9I and I10L dramatically changed the specificity of LH5: LH5-L9I cooperated with the hEPOR and not the mEPOR, and LH5-I10L cooperated with the mEPOR but not the human receptor.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Highly specific protein-protein interactions can be fine-tuned by changing the position of a single side chain methyl group at specific positions in a short TM protein with minimal chemical complexity.
source: These results demonstrate that highly specific protein-protein interactions can be fine-tuned by changing the position of a single side chain methyl group at specific positions in a short TM protein with minimal chemical complexity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutational analysis data.

claim: The ability of the traptamers to discriminate between the hEPOR and the mEPOR was determined by the amino acid sequence of the EPOR TMD.
source: Thus, the ability of the traptamers to discriminate between the hEPOR and the mEPOR was determined by the amino acid sequence of the EPOR TMD.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with chimeric EPORs shown in Figure 2D.

claim: EPO treatment or expression of LH5 caused tyrosine phosphorylation of both hEPOR and mEPOR.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, there was little, if any, tyrosine phosphorylation of either hEPOR or mEPOR in cells expressing the empty vector (lane 1). EPO treatment (lane 2) or expression of LH5 (lane 3) caused tyrosine phosphorylation of both hEPOR and mEPOR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: LH5-L9I caused tyrosine phosphorylation of hEPOR but not mEPOR.
source: LH5-L9I caused tyrosine phosphorylation of hEPOR but not mEPOR (lane 4), and LH5-I10L (lane 5) caused tyrosine phosphorylation of mEPOR but not hEPOR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: EPOR tyrosine phosphorylation correlated perfectly with the ability of the traptamers to induce growth factor independence.
source: Thus, EPOR tyrosine phosphorylation correlated perfectly with the ability of the traptamers to induce growth factor independence.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the phosphorylation data with the growth data.

claim: EPO treatment or expression of LH5 caused phosphorylation of JAK2 in cells expressing either hEPOR or mEPOR.
source: Compared to unstimulated cells (lane 1), EPO treatment (lane 2) or expression of LH5 (lane 3) caused phosphorylation of JAK2 in cells expressing either hEPOR or mEPOR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: LH5-L9I induced JAK2 phosphorylation only in cells expressing the hEPOR.
source: In contrast, LH5-L9I induced JAK2 phosphorylation only in cells expressing the hEPOR (lane 4), and LH5-I10L induced phosphorylation of JAK2 only in cells expressing the mEPOR (lane 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The traptamers specifically activate the EPOR signaling pathways to induce growth factor independence.
source: Taken together, these data show that the traptamers specifically activate the EPOR signaling pathways to induce growth factor independence.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phosphorylation and growth data.

claim: FLAG-tagged traptamers displayed the same specificity as their untagged counterparts.
source: FLAG-tagged traptamers were expressed in BaF3 cells together with hEPOR or mEPOR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and displayed the same specificity as their untagged counterparts (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The activity of the tagged traptamers implies that they adopt a type II TM orientation (i.e., N-terminus in the cytoplasm).
source: The activity of the tagged traptamers implies that they adopt a type II TM orientation (i.e., N-terminus in the cytoplasm), because it is unlikely that the highly charged N-terminal FLAG tag can cross the membrane when the traptamers are expressed in cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the FLAG tag and the activity of the tagged traptamers.

claim: Anti-FLAG antibody co-immunoprecipitated the HA-tagged hEPOR and mEPOR when FLAG-tagged LH5 was expressed in the cells.
source: In contrast, anti-FLAG antibody co-immunoprecipitated the HA-tagged hEPOR and mEPOR when FLAG-tagged LH5 was expressed in the cells (lane 4), showing that LH5 was indeed in a physical complex with the EPOR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The ability of the LH5 mutants to bind hEPOR or mEPOR correlated with their biological activity.
source: Strikingly, the ability of the LH5 mutants to bind hEPOR or mEPOR in this assay correlated with their biological activity (Figure 3C): LH5-L9I bound to only hEPOR (lane 6), and LH5-I10L bound to only mEPOR (lane 8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: LIL traptamers induce EPOR activation through binding to the EPOR.
source: These results strongly suggest that LIL traptamers induce EPOR activation through binding to the EPOR, and that the ability of the LH5 mutants to activate only one form of the EPOR is due to specific binding of the mutants to the hEPOR or mEPOR.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: LH5 and LH5-L9I induce hEPOR oligomerization.
source: As shown in lanes 5 and 6 of Figure 3D, top panel, Δ259 was indeed observed in C-20 immunoprecipitates from cells expressing traptamer LH5 and LH5-L9I, the two traptamers that interact with hEPOR. In contrast, little if any Δ259 was co-immunoprecipitated from cells infected with MSCVp empty vector (lane 4) or expressing LH5-I10L (lane 7), which does not interact with the hEPOR. These results demonstrate that the two traptamers that activate the hEPOR, LH5 and LH5-L9I, induce hEPOR oligomerization, presumably dimerization, whereas LH5-I10L does not.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The hEPOR TMD weakly dimerizes in C14SB detergent micelles.
source: Earlier work showed that the EPOR TMD weakly dimerizes in C14SB detergent micelles, and similar to other TMDs its monomer-dimer equilibrium is determined by the protein-to-detergent ratio (Ebie and Fleming, 2007; Mineev et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ebie and Fleming, 2007 and Mineev et al., 2014.

claim: A change in DHPC concentration caused a change in the monomer-dimer equilibrium of hEPOR217-277.
source: The overlay of spectra at high (red) and low (black) DHPC concentrations showed clear changes in amide backbone chemical shifts (representative residues shown in Figure 4B). Thus, a change in equilibrium occurred, likely reflecting a switch of the hEPOR TMD to a more monomeric state at increasing DHPC.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Addition of LH5 caused the chemical shifts of hEPOR217-277 to change in the opposite direction as increasing DHPC.
source: The same resonances were affected by DHPC increase (red) or LH5 addition (blue), but in opposite directions (Figure 4B and C). Thus, these treatments most likely induce opposite changes in hEPOR217-277, with DHPC pushing the equilibrium toward the monomer and LH5 pushing it toward the dimer.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: LH5 and LH5-L9I induced larger chemical shift changes in hEPOR217-277 than LH5-I10L.
source: In accordance with the inability of LH5-I10L to cooperate with the hEPOR, this peptide induced the smallest chemical shift changes, whereas LH5-L9I and LH5, which cooperate with hEPOR, induced larger changes, illustrated for Leu230 and Ala245 in Figure 4D.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: All three peptides enhance dimerization of the hEPOR TMD, but LH5 and LH5-L9I were more active at inducing dimerization.
source: These experiments indicate that all three peptides enhance dimerization of the hEPOR TMD, but the LH5 and LH5-L9I peptides were more active at inducing dimerization, consistent with the ability of the corresponding traptamers to cooperate with the hEPOR.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the NMR data.

claim: The NMR shifts induced by traptamers were saturable at a traptamer-to-EPOR TMD ratio approaching 2.
source: As shown in Fig, 4E, the NMR shifts were clearly saturable at a traptamer-to-EPOR TMD ratio approaching 2 (as it would be for the 4:2 complex).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The saturability of the NMR shifts shows that the traptamers directly interact with the EPOR TMD rather than having an indirect effect.
source: Importantly, the saturability of this process shows that we observe a direct interaction rather than an indirect effect upon addition of LH5.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the saturation data.

claim: The traptamers directly stabilize the dimeric form of the hEPOR TMD.
source: We thus conclude that the traptamers directly stabilize the dimeric form of the hEPOR TMD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the NMR data showing specificity and saturability.

claim: The ability of a traptamer to cooperate with the hEPOR was determined solely by the presence of an isoleucine at position 10.
source: The ability of a traptamer to cooperate with the hEPOR was determined solely by the presence of an isoleucine at position 10. Traptamers with an isoleucine at this position cooperated with the hEPOR, whereas mutants containing a leucine, valine, or alanine at position 10 displayed little if any ability to cooperate with the hEPOR (Figure 5, top panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Position 10 was a prime determinant of activity with the mEPOR.
source: Position 10 was also a prime determinant of activity with the mEPOR (Figure 5, bottom panel). Traptamers with leucine in position 10 cooperated with the mEPOR, regardless of the amino acid at position 9.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The amino acid at position 10 was the prime determinant of specificity.
source: Thus, the amino acid at position 10 was the prime determinant of specificity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutational analysis data in Figure 5.

claim: The S238L mutation in the mEPOR completely abrogated the ability of the mEPOR to respond to LH5-I10L.
source: In contrast, the S238L mutation completely abrogated the ability of the mEPOR to respond to LH5-I10L, showing that Ser238 was important for specific recognition of the mEPOR by LH5-I10L (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: LH5-I10L induced IL-3 independence in cells expressing the L238S hEPOR but not wild-type hEPOR.
source: As shown in Figure 6C, left panel, LH5-I10L induced IL-3 independence in cells expressing the L238S hEPOR but not wild-type hEPOR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The absence of serine at position 238 in the TMD of hEPOR is the sole reason why hEPOR does not respond to LH5-I10L.
source: Thus, the absence of serine at position 238 in the TMD of hEPOR is the sole reason why hEPOR does not respond to LH5-I10L.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutational analysis data.

claim: LH5-I10L induced IL-3 independence with the wild-type mEPOR and with the S238A and S238G mEPOR mutants.
source: Traptamer LH5-I10L induced IL-3 independence with the wild-type mEPOR and with the S238A and S238G mEPOR mutants. Thus, alanine or glycine can replace serine at position 238, demonstrating that the serine hydroxyl group is not important for activity in this assay.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: LH5-I10L did not cooperate with the S238T mEPOR mutant.
source: In contrast, LH5-I10L did not cooperate with the S238T mEPOR mutant, suggesting that the size of the side chain at position 238, rather than hydrophilicity, determined the ability of LH5-I10L to productively interact with the mEPOR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: LH5-I10S cooperated with mEPOR/S238L to restore a significant level of IL3-independence.
source: As shown in Figure 6E (left panel), LH5-I10S did not cooperate with wild-type mEPOR to induce IL-3 independence. Strikingly, however, LH5-I10S cooperated with mEPOR/S238L to restore a significant level of IL3-independence (Figure 6E, left panel, black bar).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Simultaneous mutation of position 10 of the traptamer and position 238 of the mEPOR restored complex formation.
source: Notably, simultaneous mutation of position 10 of the traptamer and position 238 of the mEPOR restored complex formation (lane 4), consistent with restoration of biological activity by this combination of mutations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Restoration of activity by compensating mutations implies that the defect of the position S238L mEPOR mutant is caused by direct disruption of the interaction with the traptamer.
source: Restoration of activity by compensating mutations also implies that the defect of the position S238L mEPOR mutant is caused by direct disruption of the interaction with the traptamer and not, for example, by an indirect effect of the mutation on the receptor itself.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the compensatory mutation data.

claim: The two proteins contact each other directly and this interaction is mediated by contacts between the side chains at position 10 in the traptamer and position 238 in the TMD of the mEPOR.
source: Taken together, these results provide strong genetic evidence that the two proteins contact each other directly and suggest that this interaction is mediated by contacts between the side chains at position 10 in the traptamer and position 238 in the TMD of the mEPOR.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the compensatory mutation data.

claim: The TMD of the mEPOR has intrinsic ability to homodimerize.
source: The TMD of the mEPOR (and to a lesser extent, the hEPOR) has intrinsic ability to homodimerize (Ebie and Fleming, 2007; Kubatzky et al., 2001; Ruan et al., 2004; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The conformational state of the dimeric EPOR TMDs regulates activity.
source: In addition to dimerization, the conformational state of the dimeric EPOR TMDs regulates activity (Moraga et al., 2015; Seubert et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moraga et al., 2015 and Seubert et al., 2003.

claim: Introduction of traptamers caused substantial remodeling of the conformational landscape of the EPOR TMD dimers.
source: Introduction of traptamers caused substantial remodeling of the conformational landscape of the EPOR TMD dimers, as it did in the other stoichiometries we tested (see Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: State III was nearly unpopulated with EPOR TMD dimers alone, but was sampled robustly in the presence of the traptamers.
source: Notably, state III was nearly unpopulated with EPOR TMD dimers alone, but was sampled robustly in the presence of the traptamers.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In state III, residue 238 of EPOR TMD mapped to a g position, making it available for quaternary interactions with traptamers.
source: In state III, residue 238 of EPOR TMD mapped to a g position, making it available for quaternary interactions with traptamers (Figure 7B; Ser238 labeled green), consistent with the experimentally-observed importance of position 238 in traptamer action.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The placement of a single side chain methyl group at traptamer position 9 or 10 affected the phase distributions.
source: Remarkably, the placement of a single side chain methyl group at traptamer position 9 or 10 affected the phase distributions. For example, state IV in the hEPOR was populated in response to LH5 and LH5-L9I, but not in response to LH5-I10L.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Positions 9 or 10 are within van der Waals contact of position 238 in 55% to 97% of all state-III trajectory snapshots.
source: In fact, analysis of simulation trajectories revealed that positions 9 or 10 are within van der Waals contact of position 238 (for at least one of the TMD helices) in 55% to 97% of all state-III trajectory snapshots, across all traptamers in all three tested stoichiometries.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Traptamers adopt a variety of orientations, yet still make specific contacts with the EPOR TMD and have a net effect of perturbing its conformational equilibrium.
source: That is, rather than being frozen in a single preferred configuration with respect to the EPOR TMD dimer, traptamers appear to adopt a variety of orientations, yet still making specific contacts with the EPOR TMD and having a net effect of perturbing its conformational equilibrium.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: MD simulations showed that traptamers rapidly inter-convert between different helical phases in all stoichiometries, such that complexes can be expected to be symmetric only in an average sense.
source: Indeed, MD simulations showed that traptamers rapidly inter-convert between different helical phases in all stoichiometries, such that complexes can be expected to be symmetric only in an average sense.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: All simulations are consistent with complexes approaching symmetry much faster than the typical ms NMR time scales.
source: In fact, analysis of our MD trajectories revealed that all simulations are consistent with complexes approaching symmetry much faster than the typical ms NMR time scales (see Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Traptamers significantly remodel the conformational landscapes of EPOR TMD dimers, shifting the populations towards states in which TMD position 238 interacted with traptamer residues 9 and 10.
source: Overall, these simulations demonstrated that traptamers significantly remodel the conformational landscapes of EPOR TMD dimers, shifting the populations towards states in which TMD position 238 interacted with traptamer residues 9 and 10.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Subtle chemical differences between traptamers can have dramatic consequences on EPOR TMD orientation.
source: Furthermore, subtle chemical differences between traptamers can have dramatic consequences on this orientation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: The EPOR TMDs remained associated with each other and with traptamers for the duration of the all-atom simulation in all systems and all replicates.
source: The EPOR TMDs remained associated with each other and with traptamers for the duration of the simulation in all systems and all replicates.
evidence: This is supported by all-atom molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Backbone RMSD of the hEPOR TMD increased significantly in the presence of the parental LH5 traptamer.
source: Backbone root-mean-square-deviation (RMSD) of the hEPOR TMD, relative to the equilibrated conformation, increased significantly in the presence of the parental LH5 traptamer, underscoring the dynamic nature of the complex, whereas the mEPOR TMD was much less dynamic than the hEPOR (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by all-atom molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The mutant traptamers caused a marked reduction in the dynamics of the hEPOR TMD along the length of the hEPOR TMD compared to LH5.
source: Compared to LH5, the mutant traptamers caused a marked reduction in the dynamics of the hEPOR TMD along the length of the hEPOR TMD (Figure 8A, top, and Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by all-atom molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 8A and 8C.

claim: The hEPOR and mEPOR TMDs responded differently to the traptamers.
source: This analysis showed that the hEPOR and mEPOR TMDs responded differently to the traptamers and that repositioning a single methyl group in a traptamer can markedly affect the dynamics of the hEPOR TMD dimer along its entire length.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the all-atom molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Repositioning a single methyl group in a traptamer can markedly affect the dynamics of the hEPOR TMD dimer along its entire length.
source: This analysis showed that the hEPOR and mEPOR TMDs responded differently to the traptamers and that repositioning a single methyl group in a traptamer can markedly affect the dynamics of the hEPOR TMD dimer along its entire length.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the all-atom molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Interactions between TMDs can display high specificity in mammalian cells that can be precisely modulated by minimal structural differences in the interacting helices.
source: By studying simple model TM proteins, we discovered that interactions between TMDs can display high specificity in mammalian cells that can be precisely modulated by minimal structural differences in the interacting helices.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: Single leucine-isoleucine substitutions at two positions in a traptamer determined whether it bound and activated the hEPOR, the mEPOR, or both receptors.
source: We discovered that single leucine-isoleucine substitutions at two positions in a traptamer, which change the placement of single methyl groups, determined whether it bound and activated the hEPOR, the mEPOR, or both receptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutational analysis and binding data.

claim: Traptamer action is mediated by direct binding to the EPOR TMD.
source: Our data show that traptamer action is mediated by direct binding to the EPOR TMD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including co-immunoprecipitation, NMR, and compensatory mutations.

claim: Direct binding of the traptamers to the EPOR is mediated by complementarity between hydrophobic surfaces generated by the sequence of leucines and isoleucines in the traptamer and the sequence of the EPOR TMD.
source: We therefore conclude that direct binding of the traptamers to the EPOR is mediated by complementarity between hydrophobic surfaces generated by the sequence of leucines and isoleucines in the traptamer and the sequence of the EPOR TMD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: There are more than 33 million possible 25-residue sequences of leucine and isoleucine.
source: There are more than 33 million (225) possible 25-residue sequences of leucine and isoleucine, suggesting that even such short, simple proteins can generate a large number of surfaces and thus potentially interact with a wide variety of target proteins.
evidence: This is a mathematical calculation based on the number of possible sequences.

claim: The traptamers act by making specific, yet dynamic, contacts with the EPOR TMDs.
source: Rather, our results strongly argue that the traptamers act by making specific, yet dynamic, contacts with the EPOR TMDs and that the amino acids at positions 9 and 10 in the traptamer and at specific positions in the EPOR TMD play key roles in this interaction, ultimately manifesting in differential ability to activate the human or mouse EPOR.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: Moving a methyl group at position 9 or 10 in LH5 one carbon closer or farther from the polypeptide backbone generates a novel surface that is now complementary to only the hEPOR or the mEPOR, thereby altering specificity.
source: Because van der Waals interactions require precise geometry and spacing, moving a methyl group at position 9 or 10 in LH5 one carbon closer or farther from the polypeptide backbone, respectively, generates a novel surface that is now complementary to only the hEPOR or the mEPOR, thereby altering specificity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of van der Waals interactions and the mutational data.

claim: The methyl group at positions 9 and 10 is acting as a molecular toggle switch to determine traptamer specificity.
source: Thus, the methyl group at these positions is acting as a molecular toggle switch to determine traptamer specificity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutational analysis data.

claim: The determinants of specificity within a membrane are controlled by minimal chemical differences.
source: The ability of a traptamer to toggle back and forth between closely related targets in response to the placement of a single methyl group implies that the determinants of specificity within a membrane are controlled by minimal chemical differences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: The LIL traptamers have lipid-like chemical properties because of their low-complexity sequence containing purely hydrocarbon side chains.
source: This observation suggests that the LIL traptamers have lipid-like chemical properties because of their low-complexity sequence containing purely hydrocarbon side chains, a feature which may favor dynamics in binding and allow for diversity in stoichiometry.
evidence: This is an inference based on the NMR data and the chemical properties of the traptamers.

claim: Traptamer:TMD complexes may form un-conventional dynamic complexes, similar to the fuzzy interactions recently described for intrinsically disordered proteins.
source: It is therefore possible that traptamer:TMD complexes form un-conventional dynamic complexes, similar to the fuzzy interactions recently described for intrinsically disordered proteins (Klein et al., 2003; Mittag et al., 2008; Olsen et al., 2017), which may nevertheless still be of high affinity.
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to work on intrinsically disordered proteins.

claim: The ability of the traptamers to productively interact in a highly specific manner with particular EPOR TMDs suggests that such dynamic interactions can also display high specificity in membranes.
source: The ability of the traptamers to productively interact in a highly specific manner with particular EPOR TMDs suggests that such dynamic interactions can also display high specificity in membranes.

claim: Traptamer binding drives the EPOR toward the oligomeric, likely dimeric, form.
source: Although the oligomerization state of the traptamer itself is not known, our co-immunoprecipitation and NMR experiments indicate that traptamer binding drives the EPOR toward the oligomeric, likely dimeric, form.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation and NMR data.

claim: Signaling by the EPOR is dependent on the orientation of its TMDs and linked cytoplasmic domains.
source: Signaling by the EPOR is dependent on the orientation of its TMDs and linked cytoplasmic domains (Moraga et al., 2015; Seubert et al., 2003; Syed et al., 1998; Remy et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: In the absence of ligand, the TMDs of the mEPOR are in an inactive orientation stabilized by hydrogen bonds across the homodimer interface.
source: In the absence of ligand, the TMDs of the mEPOR are in an inactive orientation stabilized by hydrogen bonds across the homodimer interface ([Ruan et al., 2004; Seubert et al., 2003; Li et al., 2015], and our MD results), but when the mEPOR dimer is in an active conformation Ser238 appears to be oriented away from this interface (Seubert et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and the MD simulation results.

claim: The traptamers not only stabilize the EPOR dimer but also cause it to adopt a productive orientation.
source: This implies that the traptamers not only stabilize the EPOR dimer but also cause it to adopt a productive orientation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known requirements for EPOR activation and the effects of traptamers.

claim: The traptamers induce a fraction of the mEPOR TMDs to re-orient from an inactive orientation into one where Ser238 engages the traptamer via van der Waals interactions.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, our implicit-membrane MD simulations indicate that the traptamers induce a fraction of the mEPOR TMDs to re-orient from an inactive orientation into one where Ser238 engages the traptamer via van der Waals interactions.
evidence: This is supported by the molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: The differential response of the mEPOR and the hEPOR to the traptamers in the all-atom MD simulations raises the possibility that there are differences in the mechanisms by which the traptamers activate the two species of the EPOR.

evidence: This is speculation based on the all-atom MD simulation data.

claim: Specificity is determined by repositioning the methyl group at only a limited number of positions in LH5, whereas mutations that inhibit activity against both EPORs are distributed throughout the sequence.
source: The results of these experiments established that specificity is determined by repositioning the methyl group at only a limited number of positions in LH5, whereas mutations that inhibit activity against both EPORs are distributed throughout the sequence.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comprehensive mutational analysis data.

claim: The interaction of LH5 with the EPOR TMD is stabilized by multiple weak van der Waals interactions along the length of the TM helices.
source: These results imply that the interaction of LH5 with the EPOR TMD is stabilized by multiple weak van der Waals interactions along the length of the TM helices, which, in aggregate, are sufficient to overcome the interhelical hydrogen bonds that stabilize the inactive conformations of the EPOR TMD.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutational analysis data.

claim: Moving a single methyl group at numerous positions can cause steric clashes that disrupt or weaken the binding of the traptamer to the TMD of both the hEPOR and the mEPOR.
source: In such an association driven by shape complementarity, moving a single methyl group at numerous positions can cause steric clashes that disrupt or weaken the binding of the traptamer to the TMD of both the hEPOR and the mEPOR.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutational analysis data and the concept of shape complementarity.

claim: Mutations at a few positions fine-tune specificity by generating surfaces that bind strongly to the TMD of only the hEPOR or the mEPOR, while retaining the ability to induce EPOR TMD dimerization and reorientation.
source: In contrast, mutations at a few positions fine-tune specificity by generating surfaces that bind strongly to the TMD of only the hEPOR or the mEPOR, while retaining the ability to induce EPOR TMD dimerization and reorientation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutational analysis data.

claim: The single leucine-isoleucine substitutions in the mutant traptamers generate conformational differences along the length of the hEPOR TMDs.
source: Interestingly, the all-atom simulations demonstrated that the single leucine-isoleucine substitutions in the mutant traptamers generate conformational differences along the length of the hEPOR TMDs, showing that the structural consequences of these seemingly simple changes can be complex.
evidence: This is supported by the all-atom molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Positions 2 and 9 are on one face of the TMD helix, and positions 3 and 10 are on a different face.
source: Because every seventh residue is on the same face of a TM coiled-coil, positions 2 and 9 are on one face of the TMD helix, and positions 3 and 10 are on a different face, implying that these two faces play particularly important roles in determining specificity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure of coiled-coils and the mutational data.

claim: The active traptamers fall into two classes: LH1 to LH4 activate only the hEPOR, and LH5 activates both hEPOR and mEPOR.
source: The active traptamers fall into two classes. LH1 to LH4 activate only the hEPOR, and LH5 activates both hEPOR and mEPOR.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data on traptamer activity.

claim: LH5 differs from the other traptamers at eleven positions, including the major specificity-determining positions 9 and 10.
source: As shown in the boxes in Figure 1B, LH5 differs from the other traptamers at eleven positions, including the major specificity-determining positions 9 and 10.
evidence: This is supported by the sequence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: These two classes of traptamers interact with the hEPOR in fundamentally different ways, presumably though the formation of different interaction surfaces or different oligomeric states.
source: These striking sequence and specificity differences suggest that these two classes of traptamers interact with the hEPOR in fundamentally different ways, presumably though the formation of different interaction surfaces or different oligomeric states.
evidence: This is speculation based on the sequence and specificity differences.

claim: Highly specific interactions can be fine-tuned by extremely subtle chemical differences confined to the membrane spanning segment.
source: By developing a genetic system to study small TM proteins consisting of only leucines and isoleucines, we discovered that highly specific interactions can be fine-tuned by extremely subtle chemical differences confined to the membrane spanning segment and that this specificity can be driven exclusively by van der Waals interactions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: This specificity can be driven exclusively by van der Waals interactions.

evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: The traptamers were not subjected to natural selection to eliminate undesired activities or interactions, implying that this high specificity is an intrinsic property of TMDs in the context of membrane lipids.

claim: The principles uncovered here are likely to apply to at least some naturally occurring TMDs.
source: Although we studied extremely simple model transmembrane proteins, the principles uncovered here are likely to apply to at least some naturally occurring TMDs.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: The TMD of the BPV E5 protein contains a stretch of 12 consecutive residues comprised exclusively of leucine and phenylalanine.
source: For example, the TMD of the BPV E5 protein contains a stretch of 12 consecutive residues comprised exclusively of leucine and phenylalanine, and the TMD of the human colony stimulating factor receptor contains a conserved homopolymeric stretch of 10 consecutive leucines.
evidence: This is a statement about the sequence of naturally occurring TMDs, supported by established knowledge.

claim: A leucine to isoleucine mutation in the middle of the PDGF β receptor TMD prevents binding of the E5 protein.
source: In addition, the TMD of the PDGF β receptor contains diverse amino acids, but a leucine to isoleucine mutation in the middle of this TMD prevents binding of the E5 protein (Edwards et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Edwards et al., 2013.

claim: Naturally occurring TMD interactions based on shape complementarity would also display very high specificity, unless there was an evolutionary advantage to relax this specificity.
source: Our results imply that naturally occurring TMD interactions based on shape complementarity would also display very high specificity, unless there was an evolutionary advantage to relax this specificity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings of the study.

claim: Incorporation of a limited number of hydrophilic amino acids into TMDs consisting of otherwise hydrophobic amino acids may allow homologous interactions with a family of related but not identical TMDs containing hydrophilic residues.
source: During evolution, incorporation of a limited number of hydrophilic amino acids into TMDs consisting of otherwise hydrophobic amino acids may allow homologous interactions with a family of related but not identical TMDs containing hydrophilic residues, or may generate higher affinity interactions, even if that comes at the cost of reduced specificity.
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary implications of the findings.

claim: Conservative polymorphisms or mutations in TMDs can have profound effects on TM protein function.
source: Our findings also show that supposedly conservative polymorphisms or mutations in TMDs can have profound effects on TM protein function and should be strictly evaluated for this possibility.

claim: Agents including small hydrophobic molecules and peptides that disrupt or modulate specific interactions between TMDs could have valuable research and applied uses.
source: Finally, our results suggest that agents including small hydrophobic molecules and peptides that disrupt or modulate specific interactions between TMDs could have valuable research and applied uses.

claim: Genetic selection of traptamers will be a powerful tool to elucidate additional rules governing transmembrane interactions and to identify lead compounds.
source: Genetic selection of traptamers will be a powerful tool to elucidate additional rules governing transmembrane interactions and to identify lead compounds for these approaches.
evidence: This is speculation about future applications of the traptamer system.
